sources.title: Thermal Protection Materials and Systems: Past and Future

claims.claim: A charring ablator changes as it heats: decomposition releases gases, leaves char behind and can allow the surface to recede, limiting the heat that reaches the spacecraft.

The presentation names convective heating as one of two primary sources of reentry heating: it comes from the flow of hot gas past the vehicle's surface and from catalytic chemical recombination reactions at the surface.
The other primary source is radiation heating from the energetic shock layer in front of the vehicle.
Heating depends on reentry speed, the vehicle's effective radius and atmospheric density.
The presentation describes ablative thermal protection as energy management through material consumption: exposed to entry heating, the material pyrolyzes (chars) and rejects heat in several ways.
One way an ablator rejects heat is the endothermic decomposition of its polymer.
Another is that ablation products blown into the boundary layer reduce convective heating.
Another is the formation of a char layer and re-radiation.
Insulative, reusable thermal protection instead manages energy through storage and re-radiation, with the material unchanged.
PICA was the enabling thermal protection material for the Stardust mission, where it was used as a single-piece heat shield.
For Orion the decision was made to use Avcoat, a material first used on Apollo.

sources.publisher: New South Wales Threatened Species Scientific Committee
sources.title: Lord Howe Island phasmid — critically endangered species listing

claims.claim: This large flightless stick insect once lived on Lord Howe Island and persisted on nearby Ball’s Pyramid. Its very restricted range is central to its conservation status.
Adult males reach 120 mm, more commonly 106 mm, and adult females reach 150 mm, more commonly 120 mm.
The phasmid is currently known only from a single site on Balls Pyramid, a rocky outcrop 23 km south east of Lord Howe Island.
The insects have been reported only from within a foraging area considered to be 30 m x 6 m.
Melaleuca howeana is likely to be the only host plant for the phasmid at this site.
The phasmid was once very common on Lord Howe Island, to the extent that it was used as bait for fishing.
The species became extinct on Lord Howe Island soon after a supply ship ran aground in 1918 and the ship rat came ashore.
It was considered extinct until live individuals were discovered on Balls Pyramid in 2001.
The wild population is estimated to be extremely low, with fewer than 50 mature individuals.
In 2003, two pairs of phasmids were collected from Balls Pyramid and a captive breeding program was started.
As of a July 2011 communication cited in the listing, there were 800 adults in captivity producing viable eggs.

sources.title: MSL10 is a high-sensitivity mechanosensor in the tactile sense of the Venus flytrap

claims.claim: A Venus flytrap's trigger hairs turn physical deflection into electrical signals. The studied mechanosensitive channel contributes to detecting weak stimuli.
The Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant that catches prey by closing its leaf blade.
The plant senses mechanical stimuli through organs called sensory hairs, six of which form on the leaf blade.
After a touch, the hair generates an action potential and a long-range calcium signal that travel to the leaf blade; the leaf moves to catch prey after two successive calcium signals.
A stimulated sensory hair typically generates a single action potential, with several in some cases, depending on the angle and angular speed of the stimulus.
The study identifies a two-step system in the sensory hairs: mechanosensing limited to the stimulated cell, then threshold-dependent firing of an action potential and spread of the calcium signal.
Weak stimuli generate only receptor potentials below the threshold; strong stimuli produce receptor potentials large enough to trigger action potentials.
DmMSL10 is a stretch-activated chloride channel that is concentrated in the outermost cells at the base of the sensory hair, called indented cells.
In plants with DmMSL10 knocked out, no action potentials were observed at bending speeds below 0.1 rad/s, while unmodified (wild-type) plants kept generating them at reduced speeds.
When ants visited the traps, the probability of a calcium signal was significantly reduced, by 18.5%, in the knockout traps.
The knockout traps also tended to close 13.3% less often when ants visited, but that difference was not statistically significant.

sources.title: Biosynthetic origin of benzoquinones in the explosive discharge of the bombardier beetle

claims.claim: The discharge contains benzoquinones. The study traced how these compounds are made in Brachinus elongatulus, distinguishing their biosynthesis from the process of ejecting the spray.
The defensive apparatus of bombardier beetles has two compartments, the reservoir and the reaction chamber.
When the beetle is challenged, muscles around the reservoir contract and send chemical precursors into the reaction chamber, where they mix with enzymes.
The result is an explosive discharge of a hot, noxious chemical spray containing two major quinones: 1,4-benzoquinone and 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone (toluquinone).
Untransformed fluid sampled from the reservoir held significant quantities of 1,4-hydroquinone and 2-methyl-1,4-hydroquinone.
It had previously been speculated that all the benzoquinones originate from one core precursor, 1,4-hydroquinone.
The researchers injected or fed Brachinus elongatulus beetles with precursors carrying stable-isotope labels.
Labeled 1,4-hydroquinone given to the beetles was converted specifically to 1,4-benzoquinone.
The compound m-cresol is metabolized to 2-methyl-1,4-hydroquinone, which is then oxidized to 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone in the hot spray.
The results show that the two quinones are products of two independent biosynthetic pathways.
The authors suggest this kind of pathway is not restricted to bombardier beetles and could well be a general pathway to benzoquinones.

sources.title: Cryoprotectants and Extreme Freeze Tolerance in a Subarctic Population of the Wood Frog

claims.claim: The studied subarctic wood frogs accumulated urea before freezing and mobilized glucose after freezing began. These solutes help protect tissues during freezing.
The wood frog (Rana sylvatica) is a North American species that ranges from the southern Appalachians to within the Arctic Circle.
Frogs native to the upper Midwestern United States and southern Canada tolerate freezing only to temperatures as low as -3 to -6°C.
Frogs from Interior Alaska readily survived experimental freezing to -16°C.
In Interior Alaska, frogs must survive extended freezing with hibernaculum (winter shelter) temperatures reaching minimums of -9 to -18°C.

The authors hypothesize that the northern frogs' extreme freeze tolerance derives in part from an enhanced cryoprotectant system: urea accumulates in autumn and early winter, before freezing, and glucose is quickly mobilized from liver glycogen after freezing begins.
Both urea and glucose reduce the amount of ice that forms in the body.
Alaskan frogs collected in late summer had plasma urea levels near 10 micromoles per milliliter.
During preparation for winter, plasma urea rose to 85.5 micromoles per milliliter in frogs that remained fully hydrated.
During experimental freezing, organs shed up to one-half (skeletal muscle) or two-thirds (liver) of their water.
Cycles of freezing and thawing, which winter-conditioned frogs readily survived, greatly increased the breakdown of liver glycogen and the delivery of glucose, but not urea, to skeletal muscle.

sources.title: Expression of the Pupal Determinant broad during Metamorphic and Neotenic Development of Xenos vesparum

claims.claim: Male and female development diverges: the male undergoes conspicuous metamorphosis, while the adult female retains juvenile features and remains mostly inside the host.
The free-living first-stage (1st instar) larvae seek a host within paper wasp nests.
On entering a host, the first-stage larva molts to a legless second-stage larva with a soft cuticle that lives inside the host.
The female produces first-stage larvae that leave through the brood canal in her extruded cephalothorax.
Male larvae in the 4th stage (4th instar) molt to form a pupa, which pushes out from the abdomen of the host.
Adult females remain larva-like and lack eyes, mouthparts, antennae, wings and external genitalia.
Females develop a cephalothorax that is pushed out through the host's cuticle, for mating and for releasing first-stage larvae.
In insects in which both sexes go through metamorphosis, the gene broad has been shown to be required for pupal development.
The researchers detected raised levels of broad in the last larval stage of males, but not of females.
The authors write that the data suggest the females' retained juvenile form (neoteny) could be linked to the suppression of pupal determination.
In the laboratory, larvae of the paper wasp Polistes dominula were infected individually in the nest.

sources.publisher: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
sources.title: Mechanisms and behavioural functions of structural coloration in cephalopods

claims.claim: Cephalopod skin combines pigment-bearing chromatophores with cells that reflect light structurally. The two mechanisms contribute different kinds of pattern and color.
A chromatophore consists of a pigment-containing sac with dozens of radial muscles attached around its edge.
The chromatophore muscles are innervated directly by the brain.
By contracting and relaxing the muscles, the pigment sac increases or decreases in area in less than a second.
By selectively expanding and retracting distinct groups of chromatophores, cephalopods can produce patterns such as bands, stripes and spots.
Iridophores contain stacks of thin plates that reflect light by thin-film interference.
With a multilayer reflector, the more oblique the angle, the shorter the peak wavelengths of the reflected light.
The final appearance of the animal is frequently the result of optical interactions between iridophores and chromatophores.
Besides iridophores, cuttlefish and octopus have another structural reflector type, leucophores, that creates bright white patterns, shapes and spots.
The leucophores of the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis have the optical properties of a perfect diffuser, appearing equally bright from all angles of view.
Cephalopods show a wide repertoire of body patterns for camouflage and signaling despite their apparent color blindness.

sources.title: Life History of the Emerald Jewel Wasp Ampulex compressa

claims.claim: The wasp uses a cockroach as a living host for its young. The host is subdued for reproduction; the attack and host handling are part of the wasp’s life cycle, not simply a means of killing prey.
Ampulex compressa is a parasitoid that develops inside the American cockroach, Periplaneta americana.
The attack has two stings: a swift sting into the thorax that briefly paralyzes the front (prothoracic) legs, then a sting into the head cavity.
The wasp can sense the location of the head ganglia through mechanical sensing in its stinger.
Venom in the head ganglia brings on behavioral changes lasting 7 to 10 days: a higher escape threshold, shorter escape distance and less spontaneous walking.
The stung cockroach becomes a lethargic and compliant, but not paralyzed, living food supply for the wasp's offspring.
The wasp leads the stung cockroach into its burrow by grasping the cockroach's shortened antennae.
The wasp lays a single egg on a mesothoracic leg (one of the middle pair), and the egg hatches three days later.
The larva develops through three stages (instars): the first two feed from outside the host and the third lives only inside it.
The cockroach stays alive through the first two larval stages and many hours into the third, as its organs are consumed selectively.
The wasp spins a cocoon and pupates inside the cockroach, and develops into an adult after several weeks.

sources.title: Experimental modelling of the growth of tubular ice brinicles from brine flows under sea ice

claims.claim: Cold dense brine flows down from sea ice. Seawater around the flow freezes into a hollow tube, through which brine can continue descending.
Ice brinicles are tubular, finger-like formations that grow downward from the underside of sea ice into the underlying seawater.
They are formed when pockets of concentrated salt brine in the sea ice are released, causing a plume of cold, dense brine to flow downward from the bottom of the ice layer.

Owing to freezing point depression, the brine may reach as low as −23 °C while remaining liquid, while the seawater is near its freezing point, about −1.8 °C; this temperature difference leads to a hollow tube of ice forming around the brine.
The hollow tube of ice can extend several meters down into the ocean, sometimes even reaching the seafloor.
Brinicles have been found in both the Arctic and Antarctic oceans.
Earlier literature also called brinicles ice stalactites; the authors argue against the term because an icicle is an ice stalactite with a different growth mechanism.
Natural brinicle growth speeds have been reported from about 0.2 to 2 cm per minute.
Both small brinicles (10 to 100 cm long) and large ones (1 to 6 m long, 5 to 25 cm wide) have been observed in McMurdo Sound, Antarctica.
The study grew brinicles in the laboratory by injecting a cold brine flow into a reservoir of less-salty water.
Growth of brinicles in a laboratory setting is highly dependent on the parameters of the experimental setup.

sources.title: Optimal Predator Risk Assessment by the Sonar-Jamming Arctiine Moth Bertholdia trigona

claims.claim: The tiger moth emits bursts of ultrasound in response to an approaching bat. Researchers tested how the moth times its clicking to features of the bat’s echolocation sequence.
Tiger moths respond to high-intensity bat calls with ultrasonic clicks.
Depending on the tiger moth species, the clicks can warn bats that the prey is toxic.
Bertholdia trigona is a sonar-jamming moth, and its clicking is paired with diving.
When a bat detects a prey echo it gradually increases its call rate, which begins the approach phase of echolocation.
The study found that moths clicked soon after bats detected and targeted them.
Moths typically clicked in response to bats in the early to middle approach phase.
Moth clicking was preceded by bat calls that increased in intensity and slightly decreased in pulse interval.
This happened when bats were at distances of 1 to 3 m.
The moths' clicking thresholds closely matched the predicted optimal thresholds for telling real threats from false threats.
In the study a real threat was a bat attacking the moth itself, and a false threat was a bat attacking a nearby moth.

sources.title: Draft genome assembly and transcriptome data of the icefish Chionodraco myersi

claims.claim: The studied Antarctic icefish lacks functional hemoglobin. It relies on oxygen dissolved in its blood, and the study examines cellular adaptations associated with this unusual physiology.
Antarctic fish of the family Channichthyidae are the only vertebrates that lack hemoglobin.
British whalers sailing the Southern Ocean named them icefish for their translucent look, which is due to the absence of respiratory pigments and to scaleless skin.
The extremely low water temperature (−1.8 °C) is considered the necessary condition for the evolutionary loss of hemoglobin in the icefish.
Oxygen solubility rises as water temperature falls, so the subzero Southern Ocean has a substantially higher concentration of dissolved oxygen than temperate waters.
The higher dissolved oxygen is not sufficient to compensate for the lack of hemoglobin.
Icefish show cardiovascular modifications, such as greater blood volume, wider capillaries and larger hearts, that offset the absence of oxygen carriers.
Icefish show extraordinarily high mitochondrial density.
Icefish have very few circulating red blood cells (erythrocytes).
Studies have asked whether the loss of hemoglobin is an adaptation to the extreme Antarctic environment or, conversely, an example of disaptation.
The study's genome comparison suggests that hemoglobin was lost through a series of deletion events, rapid sequence divergence, or both.

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
sources.title: Shifting mirrors: adaptive changes in retinal reflections to winter darkness in Arctic reindeer

claims.claim: The reflecting layer behind the retina is golden in summer and blue in winter. Its winter state is associated with greater visual sensitivity under dim conditions.
The tapetum lucidum works as a mirror, giving a second opportunity for photon capture by reflecting light back through the retina, which enhances visual sensitivity.
The experiments were carried out at the University of Tromsø, Norway (70° N).
The wavelength the tapetum reflects depends on the spacing of its collagen, with reduced spacing giving shorter wavelengths.
The measured spacing between collagen fibers was 26 nm in winter eyes and 43.1 nm in summer eyes.
More than 95% of the light was reflected directly back in summer eyes, compared with only 40% in winter eyes.
Winter animals have significantly increased pressure inside the eye, probably produced by permanent pupil dilation blocking the eye's drainage.
When a summer tapetum was covered with a cover slip and an 8 g weight was applied, its reflection changed to blue immediately.
The shift to a blue reflection may scatter light through the photoreceptors instead of reflecting it directly, raising retinal sensitivity through increased photon capture.
Increased sensitivity comes at the cost of reduced acuity, but may be an important adaptation for reindeer to detect moving predators in the dark Arctic winter.
The authors stress that they have not proved the functional relationships between these changes.

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
sources.title: Tales from the crypt: a parasitoid manipulates the behaviour of its parasite host

claims.claim: An infected gall wasp can stop with its head blocking its exit tunnel. The parasitoid later escapes through the host; the precise mechanism behind the behavior remains uncertain.
The host, the crypt gall wasp Bassettia pallida, is found on sand live oaks (Quercus geminata) and southern live oaks (Quercus virginiana) in the southeastern USA.
The stem galls, called crypts, are tiny compartments in which B. pallida develops before it excavates through the stem to emerge as an adult.
The researchers named the parasitoid the crypt-keeper wasp, Euderus set, after Set, the Ancient Egyptian god of evil and chaos.
When parasitized by E. set, adult B. pallida excavate an emergence hole in the crypt wall, plug the hole with their head and die.
Euderus set emerges through the host's head capsule when it reaches its adult stage.
The researchers never observed the egg stage of the parasitoid.
The parasitoid appears to infect the adult stage of the host.
In the experiment, E. set that had to excavate an emergence hole themselves were about three times more likely to die trapped in the crypt.
The authors describe working out the specific induction methods, beyond the presence of E. set, as the next step.
The authors report an observation that suggests variability in the ability of E. set to manipulate its host.

Strong updrafts can keep developing hail suspended while more ice accumulates. The layers reflect changes in how the ice grew, but they are not a precise map of the hailstone’s path through the storm.
Hail is solid precipitation in the form of balls or pieces of ice known as hailstones.
Hail develops in thunderclouds, where strong updrafts (rising air currents) and downdrafts (falling air currents) move water droplets up and down through the cloud.
When the droplets reach the top of the cloud, they freeze due to the cold temperatures.
Powerful updrafts can keep hailstones suspended for a long time, allowing them to grow larger as more layers of ice accumulate.
When hailstones become too heavy for the updrafts to support, they fall to the ground as solid balls of ice.
Unlike snow, which can form in various weather conditions, hail only forms in these convective clouds.
Hailstones are typically spherical or conical, ranging from 5 mm to over 50 mm in diameter, though most are smaller than 25 mm.
The Met Office says the largest hailstones form in multicell storms, which are more common in places like the United States.

sources.title: Male eyespan and resource ownership affect contest outcome in the stalk-eyed fly, Teleopsis dalmanni

claims.claim: The study linked contest outcome to both male eyespan and whether the fly already held the resource. Eye span is therefore not the only factor to consider when interpreting a contest.

sources.title: Review of vibrational communication and parental care

claims.claim: Thornbug offspring can send coordinated vibrations through the host plant when disturbed. Studies of Umbonia crassicornis report that these signals evoke a defensive response from the mother.
Juvenile thornbug treehoppers (Umbonia crassicornis) evoke maternal defense with group vibrational signals.
Thornbug juveniles often continue signaling after attacks end, which produces false alarms unless maternal signals inhibit them.
Female thornbug treehoppers, like female oak treehoppers, defend offspring against invertebrate predators with kicks and wing-buzzes.
In oak treehoppers, Platycotis vittata, mothers and clustered offspring communicate with one another during predator encounters through vibrations in the plant.
The paper's field playback experiment on oak treehoppers showed that offspring vibrational signals evoke maternal defense and that maternal signals can inhibit offspring signaling.
Oak treehopper offspring produced very few signals after attacks ended.
